scimon.text: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Nominal Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 (at.%) high-entropy alloy, vacuum-arc melted and cast, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h under Ar, hot-forged, re-homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, and water-quenched; specimens were cut from the resulting plate.
hidden_target.intervention: Specimens were annealed under Ar at 1100 °C for 1 h or at 1200 and 1300 °C for 30 min, then water-quenched, to determine temperature-dependent phase stability, cooling-induced transformation pathways, microstructure, and hardness.
hidden_target.conditions: Annealing was performed at 1100–1300 °C under argon, followed by rapid water quenching to room temperature. Rockwell C hardness was measured using a 1471 N load and 5 s dwell, with five indentations per condition. Phase and microstructure characterization used XRD, SEM, SADP/dark-field TEM, and STEM–EDS.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: A hierarchical, reciprocal BCC/B2 microstructure: a Ni–Al-lean, Co–Cr–Fe-rich BCC matrix containing Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 nanoparticles and larger B2 particles, while the larger B2 particles themselves contain Ni–Al-lean BCC nanoparticles. Minor FCC, including grain-boundary Widmanstätten side-plates, was also present. Higher annealing temperature produced a larger BCC fraction and a higher reported density of ordered B2 precipitates.
hidden_target.mechanism: During cooling, the high-temperature disordered BCC phase first separates within a miscibility gap into Ni–Al-lean BCC1 and Ni–Al-rich BCC2 by spinodal decomposition. The authors infer that these products undergo independent, possibly repeated sequential spinodal decompositions as cooling continues. Below the ordering transition temperature, Ni–Al-rich BCC products order into B2. Ni–Al co-clustering and ordering therefore drive chemical partitioning and reciprocal BCC/B2 phase distributions; the resulting phase boundaries, compositional modulation, and ordered domains impede dislocation motion and increase hardness.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to quenching from the lower annealing temperature, quenching from progressively higher temperatures should yield a larger BCC fraction, more pronounced spinodal/ordering features and ordered B2 precipitates, and therefore higher hardness.
hidden_target.baseline: The 1100 °C annealed-and-water-quenched condition, which had a near-equal BCC/FCC high-temperature phase mixture and the lowest measured hardness, serves as the temperature-series baseline; the undecomposed high-temperature BCC state serves as the structural baseline for the proposed cooling transformation.
hidden_target.boundary: The reported trend applies to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 annealed between 1100 and 1300 °C and then water-quenched. The alloy was inferred to be single-phase BCC at 1300 °C, whereas at 1100–1200 °C BCC and FCC coexist and FCC becomes more abundant as temperature decreases. Detailed higher-order sequential decomposition branches and nanoparticle compositions remain proposed or uncertain because nanoscale EDS could not isolate them accurately.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: Rockwell C hardness across the three quench temperatures, combined with XRD/SEM determination of BCC and FCC fractions, B2 superlattice reflections and dark-field TEM imaging of BCC/B2 distributions, and STEM–EDS mapping/line scans testing Ni–Al enrichment versus Co–Cr–Fe enrichment.
hidden_target.actual_result: Hardness increased monotonically from 38.96 ± 0.38 HRC after 1100 °C annealing to 42.82 ± 0.31 HRC after 1200 °C and 50.42 ± 0.56 HRC after 1300 °C. The 1300 °C-quenched alloy contained a major BCC phase and minor FCC, with approximately 50 vol.% fine B2 particles in the BCC matrix; B2 particles were about 50–100 nm and B2 nanoparticles in the matrix about 2–10 nm. At 1200 °C, cuboidal B2 particles were about 100 nm and spherical nanoparticles about 2–15 nm. For the 1300 °C condition, the matrix composition was approximately Cr49Co19Fe20Ni11Al1 and the fine-particle composition Cr14Co13Fe12Ni38Al23, confirming reciprocal partitioning. The matrix was predominantly BCC with minor B2 nanoparticles, whereas fine particles were predominantly B2 with minor BCC nanoparticles, consistent with sequential spinodal decomposition followed by Ni–Al ordering.
